challenges.headline: One contract, one invoice assumed
challenges.premise: The request treats contract signature as producing a single invoice.
challenges.alternative: Modeling the contract-to-invoice relationship as one-to-many from the start (milestones, recurring or partial billing) avoids a rebuild once real billing schedules surface.
challenges.consequence: Building a single-invoice write now, then discovering contracts bill on a schedule, means re-architecting the trigger and data model rather than extending it.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether any contract types bill in installments or on a recurring basis before designing the trigger.

challenges.headline: Immediate issuance, no review
challenges.premise: The invoice is implicitly created and presumably issued the moment the contract is signed.
challenges.alternative: Landing the auto-created invoice as a draft, visible to a defined owner, before it is finalized keeps a human checkpoint on figures that came from an automated source.
challenges.consequence: Issuing immediately with no review means a wrong amount, VAT rate or numbering goes out uncaught, and correcting an issued invoice is a formal act, not an edit.
challenges.recommendation: Decide the invoice's initial status (draft vs issued) and who can see/edit it before build, not during acceptance testing.

challenges.headline: Signature event fires only once
challenges.premise: The signature event is assumed to trigger invoice creation cleanly, a single time.
challenges.alternative: Treating re-signature (e.g. via an amendment) and any repeated firing of the same event as expected inputs, guarded by an idempotency check, avoids silent duplicate invoices.
challenges.consequence: Without a guard, an amendment or a re-fired event creates a second invoice against the same contract, which is a compliance and reconciliation problem once legal numbering is involved.
challenges.recommendation: Define what counts as a duplicate trigger and build the idempotency check as part of the initial scope, not as a fix later.

challenges.headline: One invoice per signature
challenges.premise: The request assumes a signed contract always produces exactly one invoice.
challenges.alternative: A contract is typically one-to-many with its invoices in this domain (milestones, recurring billing, partial invoicing), so the design should model a billing schedule from the outset, even if today it only ever emits one invoice.
challenges.consequence: If a billing schedule turns out to be needed later, a single-invoice data model has to be re-architected rather than extended, likely after invoices already exist against it.

challenges.headline: Signature event fires once
challenges.premise: The automation assumes the contract-signed event fires exactly once and safely produces one invoice.
challenges.alternative: Building creation as idempotent — keyed to the contract and its signature version — makes any retry or amendment-triggered re-signature a safe no-op instead of a second document.
challenges.consequence: Without that guarantee, a retried event or an amendment that re-opens signature can create a duplicate invoice, requiring a manual credit note to fix.
challenges.recommendation: Define the idempotency key and the intended behavior when an amendment re-signs a contract before building the trigger.

challenges.headline: Uniform billing rule assumed
challenges.premise: The request implies a single rule for deriving amount, VAT, numbering and payment terms, with no mention of variation.
challenges.alternative: Since this is a configurable multi-client platform where billing rules already vary by client, treating the derivation as configurable from day one avoids a rebuild the moment a second client needs different VAT or numbering conventions.
challenges.consequence: Hardcoding the derivation for the first client risks discovering mid-rollout that another client's invoicing rule doesn't fit, forcing rework under pressure.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client directly whether this rule is expected to be uniform or client/country-specific before deciding on a hardcoded vs. configurable design.

challenges.headline: One contract, one invoice
challenges.premise: The request treats 'contract signed' as producing exactly one invoice.
challenges.alternative: Contracts on this platform are commonly one-to-many with their invoices — milestones, recurring billing, partial payments. The automation should resolve a billing plan, not just fire a single document.
challenges.consequence: Building a single-document trigger now means redesigning the automation entirely the first time a milestone or recurring contract appears.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether any contract type requires multiple invoices before scoping the trigger.

challenges.headline: Instant creation on signature
challenges.premise: The request implies invoice creation happens right at the moment of signature.
challenges.alternative: An async, queued creation with a visible 'pending' state lets the system tolerate incomplete billing data and re-signature (amendments) without blocking the signing action or double-firing.
challenges.consequence: A synchronous, blocking trigger can fail visibly in the signer's face if contract data is incomplete, and has no natural guard against amendments re-triggering a second invoice.
challenges.recommendation: Decide sync-vs-async explicitly and design an idempotency key on the signature event before building the trigger.

challenges.headline: Direct issuance, no review
challenges.premise: The request doesn't mention any review step — invoices seem expected to appear ready-made.
challenges.alternative: Generating the invoice as a draft that a controller reviews before issuance fits the platform's existing draft → issued → paid lifecycle and catches wrong amounts or VAT before they reach a client.
challenges.consequence: Auto-issuing directly means any error in the amount source or numbering goes out the door immediately, with legal numbering consequences once it's issued.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm who, if anyone, reviews the auto-generated invoice before it counts as issued.
